Nero's persecution in Rome

After the great fire of July AD 64, Nero blames the Christians. Some are arrested and inform on many others. Victims are torn by dogs, crucified, or burned as torches at night (Tacitus, Annals 15.44). Christian tradition places the deaths of Peter and Paul in Nero's reign.
The Jewish revolt begins

Riots follow the governor Florus' seizure of temple money. The priests stop the daily sacrifice offered for the emperor, which Josephus calls the start of the war (Josephus, Jewish War 2.17.2). Factions also fight one another.
Cestius Gallus withdraws; flight to Pella

In November AD 66 the Syrian governor Cestius Gallus attacks Jerusalem, then suddenly withdraws and is routed at Beth-horon (Josephus, Jewish War 2.19.7-9). Eusebius says the Jerusalem church, warned by a revelation, left the city before the war and settled in Pella beyond the Jordan (Eusebius, Church History 3.5.3). Many see this pause as the signal Luke 21:20-21 describes.
Vespasian takes command
Nero sends Vespasian with his son Titus. In AD 67 they subdue Galilee, and Josephus himself is captured at Jotapata (Josephus, Jewish War 3.7).
Nero dies
Vespasian takes much of Judea and Peraea. Nero dies in June AD 68, and Vespasian pauses the campaign while Rome falls into turmoil (Suetonius, Nero 49; Josephus, Jewish War 4.9.2).
The year of four emperors

Galba, Otho and Vitellius rise and fall in quick succession. In July AD 69 the eastern legions proclaim Vespasian emperor, and he wins (Tacitus, Histories 2.79-81; Suetonius, Vespasian 6). Inside Jerusalem, rival factions fight each other.
Titus begins the siege at Passover

In spring AD 70, shortly before Passover, Titus camps before Jerusalem with four legions, one of them on the Mount of Olives (Josephus, Jewish War 5.2.3 and 5.3.1). Pilgrims crowd the city, and famine soon follows (Jewish War 5.12.3; 6.3.4).
The Antonia fortress falls
In July AD 70 Roman troops take the Antonia fortress beside the temple by a night attack, and Titus orders it torn down to open a way to the temple courts (Josephus, Jewish War 6.1.7-8 and 6.2.1).

On the 17th of Panemus, in mid-summer AD 70, the daily sacrifice fails for lack of men to offer it (Josephus, Jewish War 6.2.1). Many readers link this with Daniel's words about the sacrifice being taken away (Daniel 9:27; 12:11).

On the 10th of Lous, the same day as the Babylonian burning (9/10 Av, about late August AD 70), a soldier throws a burning brand into the temple and it is destroyed (Josephus, Jewish War 6.4.5-8). The soldiers then set up their eagle standards in the court and sacrifice to them (Jewish War 6.6.1).

On the 8th of Gorpiaeus (September AD 70) the upper city is taken and the whole city falls (Josephus, Jewish War 6.8.5). Josephus counts 97,000 captives and 1,100,000 dead during the war and siege (Jewish War 6.9.3). Titus orders the city and temple razed, leaving only three towers and part of the wall (Jewish War 7.1.1).

Vespasian and Titus celebrate a triumph in Rome. The golden table and the lampstand from the temple are carried in the procession (Josephus, Jewish War 7.5.5). The Arch of Titus, set up after his death in AD 81, still shows the scene.
Masada falls

The last rebel stronghold, Masada by the Dead Sea, falls to the Roman governor Flavius Silva in AD 73 or 74. Josephus says the defenders took their own lives rather than be captured (Josephus, Jewish War 7.8-9).

'Double fulfilment' is the idea that a prophecy can be fulfilled twice: once in the first century, and again on a larger scale at the end of history. Many futurist and some other readers apply this to Matthew 24. They accept that AD 70 fulfilled part of it, but expect a second and greater fulfilment before Christ returns. The fulfilled reading rejects this for Matthew 24. It holds that Jesus gave one prophecy, with one time limit, to one generation, and that it was fulfilled once. It also has a practical concern. If believers expect a repeat, they may wait in fear for disaster instead of serving Christ with confidence now.
Sealed for later, unsealed for now

Daniel was told to seal up his vision because it referred to many days in the future, until 'the time of the end'. John was told the opposite: do not seal the prophecy, because the time is near. The fulfilled reading sees Revelation as the opening of what Daniel sealed. On this view, the 'time of the end' is the end of Israel's old covenant age, not the end of time, and it had arrived in John's day.
One generation, one time limit

Jesus said that 'this generation' would not pass away until all these things happened. He did not say that some things would happen then and the rest later. The same phrase in Matthew 23:36 clearly means the people He was speaking to. A second fulfilment, the reading argues, would need a second time limit, and the text gives none.
A tribulation that cannot happen again

Jesus said the great tribulation would be worse than anything before it 'or ever shall be'. If it can never be equalled, the reading argues, it cannot be repeated on a larger scale later. It happened once, in the disciples' generation.
The temple and its system are gone

The prophecy is tied to a particular building, city and land: the holy place, Judea, Sabbath travel and flat housetops. Hebrews says the old covenant was becoming obsolete and ready to vanish away. The fulfilled reading holds that God's dwelling is now His people, so there is no need for another temple to be defiled or destroyed.
Once, at the end of the ages

Christ appeared once at the end of the ages to put away sin. The great saving events, His birth, death, resurrection and the giving of the Spirit, are not repeated. The fulfilled reading places the close of the old covenant age with these once-for-all events. Paul could say that the ends of the ages had come on his own generation.

Those who hold to multiple or typological fulfilment make a serious case. First, prophecy often has near and far horizons. Isaiah 7:14 had a sign for King Ahaz, yet Matthew 1:23 sees its fullest meaning in Jesus. Joel 2 was fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:16-21), but its signs in the sun and moon may also point further. Second, the 'abomination of desolation' itself shows a pattern. Daniel's words were first fulfilled when Antiochus IV defiled the temple in 167 BC (1 Maccabees 1:54), yet Jesus applied them to a later event. If one prophecy can be fulfilled more than once, the same may be true of Jesus' own words. Third, some features of the discourse seem wider than AD 70: the coming like lightning seen from east to west, the gathering of the elect from the four winds, and the final judgment of all nations in Matthew 25:31-46. Fourth, Luke speaks of Jerusalem trampled 'until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled' (Luke 21:24), which suggests a long period after AD 70. Many partial preterists and amillennial readers see AD 70 as a real, God-given preview of the final judgment, a type of the last day rather than its replacement. For them, the fall of Jerusalem shows how certainly Christ's final coming will also arrive.
John's age

John is told he must prophesy again about many peoples, nations and kings (Revelation 10:11). Early-date writers argue that this fits a man in his sixties, writing in the late 60s, better than a man past ninety in AD 95-96.

Late-date scholars reply that the verse may mean John's written prophecy would reach the nations, not that he would travel. Early church writers also describe John working in Ephesus as a very old man, into the reign of Trajan (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5 and 3.3.4; Clement of Alexandria, Who Is the Rich Man 42).

Revelation is written to seven real churches in Asia (Revelation 1:4). Some early-date writers argue that this list fits the 60s, after an earthquake struck Laodicea and its neighbours, Colossae and Hierapolis, around AD 60 (Tacitus, Annals 14.27). The coming "hour of trial" (Revelation 3:10) would then be the Neronian persecution and the war that followed.

Late-date scholars note that seven is a number of completeness in Revelation, and that other churches in Asia existed at the time (Acts 20:5; Colossians 4:13). Laodicea rebuilt quickly and is called rich (Revelation 3:17). Polycarp's letter may suggest that the church at Smyrna did not yet exist when Paul wrote (Polycarp, Philippians 11.3), and Ephesus has lost its first love (Revelation 2:4). They take both points as signs of a later date.
The temple still standing

John is told to measure the temple and altar, while the outer court is given to the nations to trample for forty-two months (Revelation 11:1-2). Early-date writers argue that this assumes the Jerusalem temple still stood. It matches Jesus' words that Jerusalem would be trampled by the Gentiles (Luke 21:24), and no New Testament text speaks of a rebuilt temple.

Late-date scholars answer that this is a vision, like Ezekiel's measured temple, which was given when the temple lay in ruins (Ezekiel 40:1-3). In Revelation the temple often stands for God's people (Revelation 3:12). A symbolic temple does not need a standing building.
The tribes of the earth

Revelation 1:7 says that those who pierced Him will see Him coming with the clouds, and the tribes of the earth will mourn. This joins Daniel 7:13 and Zechariah 12:10, the same texts behind Matthew 24:30. The apostles laid the guilt of the crucifixion on Jerusalem's leaders of that generation (Acts 2:36; 1 Thessalonians 2:14-15), and the Greek word for earth can mean the land. So early-date writers take the book's theme to be a coming in judgment on that generation, which would only make sense before AD 70.

Late-date scholars note that Revelation adds "every eye" and often uses "tribes" and "earth" for all peoples (Revelation 5:9; 7:9). They also note that the verse tells us the book's theme, not the year it was written.
The woman and the great city

The great city is "where also their Lord was crucified" (Revelation 11:8). Babylon is drunk with the blood of the saints and prophets (Revelation 17:6; 18:24), the same blood-guilt Jesus laid on Jerusalem (Matthew 23:35-37). The prophets had called Jerusalem "Sodom" (Isaiah 1:10). So early-date writers identify Babylon as Jerusalem, judged in AD 70.

Many scholars point out that the woman sits on seven hills and rules over the kings of the earth (Revelation 17:9, 17:18), which fits Rome. After AD 70 Jewish writers used "Babylon" as a name for Rome because Rome, like Babylon, had destroyed the temple (4 Ezra, 2 Baruch, Sibylline Oracles 5). Late-date scholars take this naming as a sign that Revelation was written after AD 70.
The sixth king: Nero

Five kings have fallen, one is, and the other has not yet come and will remain a short time (Revelation 17:10). Counting from Julius Caesar, as Suetonius and Josephus do, the five are Julius, Augustus, Tiberius, Gaius and Claudius. The sixth, who "is", would be Nero (AD 54-68), and the short seventh would be Galba, who ruled about seven months. On this count John wrote while Nero reigned.

Others begin with Augustus, or skip the three short reigns of AD 68-69, which can lead to Vespasian or Domitian. Many take the seven kings as a symbol of the whole line of world empires. Many late-date scholars also link the beast who "was, and is not" (Revelation 17:8, 17:11) to the legend that Nero would return, which spread after his death.
The song of Moses

Those who overcome the beast sing the song of Moses (Revelation 15:3). Early-date writers link this to Deuteronomy 32, a song about Israel in the latter days, about a perverse generation and about God avenging the blood of His servants (Deuteronomy 31:29; 32:5, 32:43). The martyrs' cry for vengeance (Revelation 6:10) fits the blood-guilt laid on Jesus' generation (Matthew 23:35). So the martyrs would be first-century believers.

Late-date scholars note that the words of the song in Revelation 15:3-4 praise God's works and say all nations will come and worship. That echoes the song of deliverance in Exodus 15 more than the judgment song of Deuteronomy 32. A song of Moses can suit persecuted believers in any period.
The time element

Revelation says its events "must shortly come to pass" and that "the time is at hand" (Revelation 1:1, 1:3; 22:6, 22:10). Daniel was told to seal his book because its time was far off (Daniel 8:26; 12:4), but John is told not to seal his. Early-date writers argue that the nearness covers the whole book and points to the fall of Jerusalem.

Futurists often read "shortly" as "swiftly once it begins", or measure it by God's time (2 Peter 3:8). Late-date scholars also note that nearness does not fix a date, since a book written in AD 95 could expect near events in Rome. They rely on the testimony of Irenaeus that the vision was seen near the end of Domitian's reign (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.30.3; Eusebius, Church History 3.18.2-3). Early-date writers reply that Irenaeus' words may mean that John, not the vision, was seen then.
The gospel was not preached to the whole world before AD 70.
Jesus did not visibly return in AD 70.
The tribulation of AD 70 was not the worst in history.
Luke 21:24 says Jerusalem will be trampled until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled. Does that not point to a long age after AD 70?
Acts 1:11 says Jesus will come back in the same way the disciples saw Him go.
If AD 70 fulfilled Matthew 24, why did the early church not say so?
What about the resurrection of the dead in 1 Corinthians 15?
"This generation" means the Jewish race, or the generation that sees the signs, not Jesus' hearers.
Revelation was written around AD 95, so its visions cannot be about AD 70.
Could AD 70 be a first, partial fulfilment, with a greater one still to come?

If the end of the age came in the first century, what now? The fulfilled reading answers by going back to the beginning. In Genesis 1:28 God blessed the first humans and gave them five commands. Sin distorted that calling, but Christ, the last Adam, restores it. Through one man's sin came condemnation, and through one man's righteousness comes life (Romans 5:18). As He is, so are we in this world (1 John 4:17). So believers are not waiting for the world to collapse. They are called to live out the original mandate under the reign of Christ, without fear of the future. Many Christians of other views also teach the creation mandate and faithful stewardship; the fulfilled reading gives it special weight because it holds that the great judgment Jesus foretold is past.
Be fruitful
Bear fruit in character and in work. Jesus said His Father is glorified when His disciples bear much fruit (John 15:8). Fruitfulness starts with a life joined to Christ.
Multiply
In Acts the word of God spread and the number of disciples multiplied. Share the faith, raise children in it, and train others who will train others (2 Timothy 2:2).
Fill (replenish)
The earth will be filled with the knowledge of the Lord's glory as the waters cover the sea. Bring the life of Christ into every place: home, work, study, art and public life.
Subdue
Subduing begins within. Bring every thought under Christ, overcome evil with good (Romans 12:21), and patiently bring order and healing where there is disorder.
Have dominion

Those who receive God's grace 'reign in life' through Jesus Christ. Dominion means caring service under the King, not control over others. Christ, who has all authority, sends His people to make disciples of the nations (Matthew 28:18-20).
Which Roman general led the siege that destroyed the temple in AD 70?
Pompey
Hadrian
Titus, son of the emperor Vespasian, commanded the siege of Jerusalem in AD 70. Pompey took the city in 63 BC, and Hadrian crushed a later revolt in AD 132-135.
Which ancient historian was an eyewitness of the siege of Jerusalem?
Tacitus
Suetonius
Josephus was with Titus during the siege as an interpreter. Tacitus and Suetonius wrote later from Rome, and Eusebius wrote more than two centuries afterwards.
When did the temple burn?
Spring of AD 66
Late summer of AD 70
Autumn of AD 73
Josephus dates the burning to the tenth day of the month Lous (Av), in late summer AD 70 (Jewish War 6.4.5). The revolt began in 66 and Masada fell in 73 or 74.
In Matthew 23:36, who are 'this generation' on whom 'all these things' will come?
The Jewish people in every age
The people living in Jesus' own day
A generation alive at the end of history
The Gentile nations
Jesus was speaking to the scribes and Pharisees in the temple. The fulfilled reading, and many other readers, take 'this generation' here as His own contemporaries.
Which four disciples asked Jesus about these things privately, according to Mark 13:3?
Peter, James, John and Andrew
Peter, Thomas, Philip and Matthew
James, John, Judas and Bartholomew
Andrew, Philip, Thomas and Matthew
Mark names Peter, James, John and Andrew, two pairs of brothers. The fulfilled reading stresses that 'you' in the discourse first means them.
Which Roman governor of Syria marched on Jerusalem in AD 66 and then suddenly withdrew?
Pontius Pilate
Felix
Cestius Gallus attacked Jerusalem in the autumn of AD 66, then withdrew and was defeated at Beth-horon (Jewish War 2.19). Many interpreters think this gave Christians a window to flee.
According to Eusebius (Church History 3.5.3), where did the Jerusalem church go before the war?
Antioch
Masada
Pella
Eusebius says the church was warned by a revelation to leave the city and settle in Pella, a town east of the Jordan. The fulfilled reading sees this as obedience to Matthew 24:16.
The Greek word for 'world' in Matthew 24:14 is oikoumene. What does it usually mean?
The planet and the stars
The inhabited world, often the Roman world
The age to come
The land of Israel only

Oikoumene means the inhabited earth. Luke 2:1 uses it for the Roman Empire. Paul could say the gospel had been proclaimed in all creation under heaven (Colossians 1:23) and in all the world (Colossians 1:6).
Which Roman historian wrote that many Jews believed ancient writings foretold men from Judea would rule the world (Histories 5.13)?
Pliny the Elder
Cassius Dio
Livy
Tacitus records this belief in Histories 5.13. Suetonius reports a similar oracle in Vespasian 4.5. Both say the Romans applied it to Vespasian.
According to Josephus (Jewish War 6.9.3), how many people were taken captive during the whole war?
Josephus gives 97,000 captives and 1,100,000 dead. Scholars debate his numbers, but these are the figures he reports.
Why was John told not to seal his prophecy (Revelation 22:10)?
Because it was secret
Because the time was near
Because Daniel had already explained it
Because it was only for Gentiles
John was told not to seal it because the time was at hand. Daniel was told to seal his vision because it referred to days far in the future (Daniel 8:26; 12:4).
Which monument in Rome shows soldiers carrying the temple lampstand in triumph?
The Colosseum
Trajan's Column
The Arch of Titus
The Pantheon
The Arch of Titus was built after Titus' death in AD 81. One relief shows the menorah and other temple objects carried in the victory parade.
What do partial preterists such as R. C. Sproul and Kenneth Gentry still expect in the future?
Nothing; all prophecy is fulfilled
A rebuilt temple in Jerusalem
The bodily return of Christ and the resurrection of the dead
A second destruction of Jerusalem
Partial preterists accept that much of Matthew 24 was fulfilled in AD 70, but with the historic creeds they expect a future bodily return, resurrection and final judgment.
Which of these is NOT one of the five commands of Genesis 1:28?
Withdraw
The five are: be fruitful, multiply, fill (replenish) the earth, subdue it, and have dominion. The fulfilled reading calls believers to live these out under Christ's reign.
